en: [ed. p. 94] 3.0 The Meditative Context:
Now, with the passage beginning with *paritaḥ* and ending with *viśvam āpūrayan*, he explains the yoga of the *bindu*.
The entire world has been rendered fully awakened by the lords of sages, who have dispelled all delusion on every side through the rays of light from their infinite hearts.
Having internalized the universe within one's own mantra. || 109 ||

109.1. By means of those lords of sages (*munīndra*) who have been emanated by the rays of light from the heart of the *jñānasattva*—and who are infinite—the entire world has been rendered perfectly awakened (*sambuddhīkṛta*). Therefore, having encompassed the whole world within one’s own mantra—that is, the mantra of the *jñānasattva* at the heart—and having realized that it is free from forms and so forth, and thus devoid of delusion on all sides, one should contemplate one’s own mind as being of the nature of the drop (*bindu*) of the excellent mantra; such is the connection.
[The Provisional Standpoint of the Vijñānavāda] 3.1. The Pūrvapakṣa (Opposing View).

110.0 But if external objects truly exist, how can the meditation on the entire universe as having been made fully awakened within the body of the seed-syllable situated upon the sword in the heart of the *jñānasattva*, and the visualization of the maṇḍala-circle of the nature of the universe within that drop, be logically established? Thinking thus, he first states the absence of any proof (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the existence of objects, beginning with the words "the form and so forth."

To state, for the time being, that there is no valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the existence of [the object] conceived [as such], he says: "That which is devoid of the forms of color and so forth is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," and so on. That which grasps it [is not perceived].
Nor is there anything to be apprehended, because no connection is perceived, nor [is it apprehended] by another.

110.1 "Free from the form of color and so forth" means that which is devoid of the aspects (*ākāra*) of color and so on; as for the claim that it is the "grasper" of those [objects], such a grasper of color and so forth is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is any object of cognition (*grāhya*) perceived by direct perception. Rather, it is only the aspect of color and so forth itself—which is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpa*), non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—that manifests as direct perception. The point is that the form of the "object of cognition" and so forth is merely constructed by the artifice of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As it has been said:
There is nothing else to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of it;
due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, it manifests by itself. (Pramāṇaviniścaya 1.38).
Likewise—

"Although the nature of cognition is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, to those whose vision is distorted. (Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa 353).
3.2.2 Refutation of the Aspect of the ‘Apprehender’ (grāhaka) 3.2.2.1 The Apprehender Intended as a Property-Bearer (Against Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika)

Now, the cognition of an object is itself the experience (*saṃvedana*), which is a property (*dharma*). How could that exist without an experiencer? For properties are seen to be dependent upon a substratum (*dharmin*), just like cooking and so forth. Therefore, this act of experiencing must necessarily have an agent—an experiencer—who serves as its locus and substratum. And that very [agent] is called the grasper (*grāhaka*). Since it has color-form and other such things as its objects, the grasped (*grāhya*) is also established.

To the objection, "In that case, since the establishment of the apprehended and the apprehender occurs through inference or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), how can there be a negation of them?", he says: "Because no connection is perceived, nor by another. The syntactical connection is: "Neither the apprehender nor the apprehended, which are devoid of forms such as color and so forth, is perceived."

This is the intended meaning: the cognition of an imperceptible object does not arise from itself through inference, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), or any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) postulated by others, for that would entail its being perceptible. Nor does it arise from another, because there is no connection; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of everyone cognizing everything. Furthermore, no infallible connection other than identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is possible. In this regard—

(i) If one accepts the essential identity (*tādātmya*) as the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then the oneness of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is indeed real; thus, there exists only the cognition of the forms of color and so forth. The distinction between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, however, is merely conceptualized because it serves as the basis for exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) according to the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of the cognizer; this is a point of agreement. (ii) But if one accepts the causal production (*tadutpatti*) as the necessary connection, then perception (*pratyakṣa*) and non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)—which are the means of ascertaining that [connection]—are impossible. For those two cannot exist with respect to a substratum (*dharmin*) that is the apprehending subject when it is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*). Consequently, even the relation of being produced from that [subject] is impossible.

Nor can the apprehender be inferred—like the eye and other sense organs—from the impossibility of the cognition of form and so forth, because the cognition bearing the aspect of form and so forth arises solely from a preceding causal complex (*kāraṇakalāpa*). Even so, if one were to admit another cause as its basis, an insurmountable consequence of infinite regress would follow. Therefore, there is no real distinction between the apprehended, the apprehender, and their cognition.

However, cooking and the like are, in the ultimate sense, merely the forms of entities arising in such and such ways, with distinctions imagined through mere conceptual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); even in those cases, there is no real distinction between action and agent in the form of property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*).

3.2.2.2 The Grasper Intended as Mind and Mental Factors (Against the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas) 111.0 [Objection: Granted that there may be no grasper distinct from cognition; however, that very cognition, being internally cognized in the form of pleasure (*sāta*) and so forth, is experienced as grasping the forms of external objects such as color-and-shape (*rūpa*). Therefore, how is non-duality established? In response to this doubt, he says: "The activity," and so forth.
The activity of pleasure and so forth...
No one has been observed to possess this [unity];
for that which is perceived simultaneously, like color-form and so forth, is not a grasper. (111)

111.1 In the apprehension of that form and so forth, no activity whatsoever is observed on the part of the experience of pleasure and so forth; for this pleasure and so forth exists as being perceived simultaneously with the form and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that it is non-apprehending, just like the form and so forth. Just as the form and so forth are not the apprehenders of pleasure and so forth—because, due to their simultaneous perception, there is an absence of the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, like the left and right horns of an ox—likewise, pleasure and so forth are also not the apprehenders of the form and so forth.

For they are indeed non-different because of the rule of simultaneous perception; however, difference is perceived by those whose vision is distorted, just as in the case of the moon appearing double—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said:
"This internal discernment appears as if it were an external part;
for the appearance of difference in non-different cognition is indeed a cognitive distortion. [Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa 212]

But surely, form and so forth first present themselves as the producers of cognition, and only afterwards does the arising of the experience of pleasure and so on occur. How then can there be simultaneous perception? To this it is replied:
[ed. p. 98] 3.2.2.3 Refutation of the Vaibhāṣikas’ Thesis that Cognitions are Devoid of the Image of Their Object (*nirākāravāda*)

If, according to the Vaibhāṣika position, consciousness is held to be formless and yet apprehends an object possessing form by way of obstructing its arising, then—since mere cognition is common to all objects—there would be no specific determination of cognition such that "this is the cognition of blue" or "this is the cognition of yellow. Consequently, one seeking the causal efficacy of coloring and so forth would not invariably engage with blue and the like; therefore, there would be no perception of the object whatsoever.

3.2.2.4 Refutation of the Sautrāntika Thesis that Cognitions are Endowed with the Image of Their Object (*sākāravāda*) Now, if—according to the Sautrāntika system—it is maintained that cognition, possessing the image of its object, becomes the apprehender of a preceding momentary object by virtue of arising from it, then at the time of the cognition, the object-moment that produced it is non-existent due to its momentariness, and because there is no perception of two distinct images, only the image of the cognition itself is perceived. Thus, the form of the object would not differ from a flower in the sky; how, then, can there be an acceptance of the object?

3.2.2.5 Refutation of Proof by Presumption (*arthāpatti*) If it is argued that the existence of an object that is eternally beyond perception is established through presumption (*arthāpatti*), on the grounds that its perception—characterized by a restriction of place, time, form, and causal efficiency—is otherwise inexplicable in the absence of an object, we say: no. Even in the absence of an external entity restricted by place and so forth, a perception restricted by place and so forth will occur due to the restriction of mental impressions (*vāsanā*), as in dreams and the like. Why then should we deceive ourselves with the postulation of an object that serves no purpose?

3.2.2.6 Refutation of the Objection that Restrictions Can Be Explained Only When External Objects Are Present, as well as the Refutation of the *Anyākāravāda* (Mīmāṃsā) i. Refuting the View that Spatial and Temporal Restrictions Occur Only When an External Object Is Present [ed. p. 99]
111.3 Now, it might be argued that even in dreams and the like, the external object seen in another place is indeed the cause. As it has been said:
"In cognitions such as dreams, an external object is by no means denied;
in every case, the external is the objective support (*ālambana*), though its nature is altered by place and time. [Ślokavārttika, Nirālambanavāda 107cd–108ab]
Thus, how can the restriction of place and so forth for consciousness occurring in the waking state be described by means of examples such as dreams?

That is incorrect, because an objective support (*ālambana*) for dream-cognition and the like is untenable. For that [dream-cognition] must be either of the nature of a direct perception (*grahaṇa*) or of the nature of a memory (*smaraṇa*). In this regard, it cannot first be a perception; for since a perception does not depend on a prior perception, there would be no fixed restriction in its grasping the object of a previous observation, just like any other [subsequent] observation. Nor is its being of the nature of a memory tenable, because it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), because its object is present, and because it appears with vivid clarity (*sphuṭābhatva*).

Therefore, we do not understand how this [cognition] can have as its object things seen in another place and so forth. (111.4) Or, let it be that [the external object] is its cause; however, it is impossible to justify that the restriction to a specific place and so on is caused by it. For if the external object were present in whatever place and so on—even in a dream—and it were to appear in that very same place, then it might be its cause. But this is not possible, because it would entail the consequence that there is no discrepancy [between the cognition and the object]. On the other hand, if it were to appear in some place entirely devoid of that [object], then it cannot logically be the cause of this [cognition].

If it were to produce a manifestation in something devoid of that form, it would do so anywhere, because there would be no distinction [between possible objects]. Furthermore, even in the absence of a common external object, a lack of restriction to a particular mental continuum is observed: for instance, when two people experience a similar dream-perception, or when many people with erroneous cognition perceive the appearance of hair and so forth.
iii. Refuting the claim that there is a restriction regarding causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) only when an external object is present. [ed. p. 100]

Likewise, even in the absence of external objects, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is indeed perceived in a dream. Just as in the waking state, causal efficiencies such as pleasure arising from a woman and the subsequent acts of emission connected to her are directly experienced, so too are they in the state of dreaming. Therefore, just as in dreams and the like, spatial restriction and other such features occur without an external object, why should those occurring in the waking state be denied?
As it has been said:
"For someone, something specific serves as the awakener of an internal latent impression (*vāsanā*)."
"Therefore, the restriction of cognitions is not dependent upon external objects. [Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa° 336].

Since that [cognition] lacks an external cause for its perception, we do not understand how the description of the fault regarding the absence of simultaneous apprehension—given the prior-posterior sequence between form (*rūpa*) and pleasure (*sātā*)—could be tenable.

But surely, even when they are perceived simultaneously, pleasure (*sātā*) and so forth—which are determined as the apprehenders by virtue of grasping form and the rest—are indeed the *grāhaka* (apprehender), whereas the object, such as form, is the *grāhya* (apprehended) because it is common to all perceivers; for it is certain that the moments of objective cognition arise from preceding causal complexes specifically as apprehended and apprehender. So how can there be a state of confusion between the apprehended and the apprehender?

This too is utterly devoid of substance, because in direct perception—which is non-conceptual—there appears neither the determination of the grasped and the grasper nor the commonality of the blue. Indeed, the fact that blue is visible to other perceivers is not accessible through direct perception, for that would entail the consequence that the perceptions of others are also directly perceived. Nor is it accessible through inference arising from signs such as the bristling of hair, because that [inference] has only universals as its object.

Therefore, it is cognition itself that is perceived simultaneously as having uncommon forms such as color and so forth, because it is known by itself even when unknown by those situated in suitable locations. [Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa° 16b2c] [ed.
p. 101] 3.2.3 Refutation of the Aspect of the ‘Apprehended’ (grāhya)

112.0 But surely, the non-momentary external object—such as a composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth—is a single entity; because it persists through prior and subsequent times, its commonality (*sādhāraṇatva*) is also known through inference, and thus [the claim] is not incoherent. In response to this doubt, he says: "And what is seen," and so forth. That which is seen as white and so forth at one time is not seen as such at other times.
Because these two are mutually contradictory, they are eternally [opposed] like pleasure and so forth. || 112 ||

112.1 That which is white and so forth, having a white form and so on, which is seen as a single entity and apprehended through direct perception—that very same thing is not seen at other times, whether before or after. The meaning is that it is seen precisely as being devoid of prior and posterior forms. He states the reason: because these two—the one already seen and the one currently being seen, or the one currently being seen and the one yet to be seen—are eternally contradictory to one another, like pleasure and pain.

For visual and other sensory consciousnesses grasp only what is proximate and present; otherwise, it would be impossible to avoid the consequence that things which are distant or obstructed, as well as those that are past, future, young, or old, would all be perceived simultaneously.
And this was stated by the Master in the *Ātmasādhanāvatāra* for the purpose of refuting external objects:

If it is asked: "How can cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), which appears in the form of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth, be of the nature of mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*)?", we reply: No, because that which is the object of cognition is not established as being the apprehended object and so forth. Indeed, apart from the appearance of form (*rūpa*) and the rest, no other apprehended object or apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is ever perceived. Furthermore, that whose essential nature is not being cognized cannot be the object of the conventional usage of "existence," for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor does the cognition of that [subject] occur through a cognition connected to it, because a connection with anything is unestablished for that which is absolutely imperceptible by its very nature.

If it is argued that pleasure (*sātādi*) and so forth, appearing internally, possess the status of the grasper (*grāhakatva*), whereas blue and so forth, characterized by being perceived as external to that [consciousness], possess the status of the grasped (*grāhyatva*), we say no; for the operation of pleasure and so forth upon blue and so forth is unestablished. Furthermore, that whose operation is not perceived cannot be called a grasper; if that were the case, it would follow that external objects such as form (*rūpa*) would also be graspers.
Indeed, when two things appear simultaneously and independently, we see no cause for a restrictive rule that one is the grasped and the other is the grasper.

The thought "I perceive blue and so forth" is also merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), because there is a cognition of things appearing internally and externally with independence. Indeed, this entire continuum of conceptualizations such as the subject (*grāhaka*) and so forth is intent upon manifesting independent experience, since it exists only when phenomena appear while devoid of any mutual operation of grasping one another. Therefore, nothing whatsoever is the grasper of anything else.

And so it has been said: "For indeed, Subhūti, one dharma does not know another dharma," and so forth (*Prajñāpāramitā*, source untraced). As for what was stated—"form is cognized by two types of consciousness," and so on (*Locus Classicus*, source untraced)—that is without fault, as it is made with reference merely to the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of that form, similar to the occasional teaching of a *pudgala* (person) and so forth.
Thus, by this much, the refutation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that would establish the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) has been demonstrated. 112.3.

3.3 Exposition of the Sublating Proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*): Things Possess Neither a Single nor a Multiple Intrinsic Nature (*svabhāva*) Now, demonstrating that things lack existence by means of a sublating proof, [the author] says: "And it is not one," and so forth.
It is not a single [nature] for form and the rest.
Because it is not perceived even as atoms when analyzed according to its distinctions such as beginning and end, it does not possess multiple forms, just like that [consciousness]. // 113 //
[ed. p.
103] 3.3.1 Refutation of External Objects: The Categories (Padārtha) of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika 3.3.1.1 Space, Time, Direction, and the Internal Organ (Antaḥkaraṇa)

113.1 This is the intended meaning. An external object (*artha*) is described by others as being of many kinds, through the distinctions of qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), and so forth. Among these, substance (*dravya*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of properties such as qualities; since those [properties] are uprooted along with their very root by the negation of that [substance], no separate refutation is stated for them. Furthermore, since there can be no inherence (*samavāya*) when there is no substratum in which things inhere, its refutation also is not mentioned separately.

Substance (*dravya*) is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, air, space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), self (*ātman*), and mind (*manas*). Among these, the self is to be refuted immediately hereafter. As for space, it is held to have sound as its quality, and it is singular. Because all sounds would occupy the same location, they could not be heard distinctly. Consequently, there would be the following certainty: either a sound located in a distant place would be heard just like one nearby, or else no other sound at all would be heard. Furthermore, because direction and time are each singular, the cognitions of "east," "west," "before," and "after" would be impossible.

It might be argued that this distinction in cognition arises from the difference between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Is the priority and posteriority of these adjuncts intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*)? In the first case, since the cognition of that [priority/posteriority] is established by those very adjuncts, these two [space and time] would be purposeless. In the second case, if it is by space and time alone, then because these two are one, this [distinction] does not cohere. If it is by something else, then the uselessness of those two remains as before.

Furthermore, these [entities]—space, direction, and time—are eternal; whether in association with auxiliary causes or in their absence, they do not undergo any change in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). How then could they produce their own effect only at certain times? For instance:
"The capacity or incapacity that resides in them by their very nature cannot be remedied because they are eternal; who is able to alter it? (Pramāṇavārttika, Pratyakṣa 22)

By this, the mind (*manas*) is also refuted. According to those who maintain the existence of the mind, the mind is to be inferred from the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions. However, cognitions are indeed experienced simultaneously during such events as watching a dancer; and this would never be possible if the mind existed as a single, unitary faculty. Therefore, space and the other [elements] do not exist at all. 3.3.1.2 Physical Elements 3.3.1.2.1 The Whole (*avayavin*)

Earth and the other elements remain. These too are conceived as being twofold, by way of the distinction between composite wholes (*avayavin*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*). Even there, neither the composite whole exists, nor do the atoms exist, because there are subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) against both. He states those very subverting arguments in their respective order: The so-called "one"—namely, the form of a composite whole such as a jar and so forth, which is well-known to be produced by atoms through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on—does not exist at all. This is because it is observed to be devoid of a single gross form, due to the presence of mutually contradictory properties such as the distinctions of beginning, end, middle, and so forth, belonging to color and the rest.

Thus, by this, non-apprehension in the form of the apprehension of an object associated with a single cognition is stated as the reason. For it is only the parts that appear, arranged here and there; moreover, another entity possessing those parts, being partless, does not manifest at all. [Dharmakīrti? Untraced]

If there were a single whole (*avayavin*), then when one part is colored or shaken, that whole—though inherent in all parts—would have to be seen as either colored or shaking. If you argue that the coloring or shaking resides in the part and not in the whole, then that whole would necessarily be seen as uncolored or unshaking. Furthermore, when one part is covered, if the whole were covered by it, it would not be seen; yet if it were not covered by it, the consequence that it would still be perceived as uncovered would be unavoidable. Therefore, because of the imposition of contradictory properties consisting of difference, there is no single whole.
[ed. p. 105] We observe that it is precisely the state of being an object of the conventional designation "non-existent" that has now arrived for this [atom], since it ought to come into being.

Now, when a single [entity] is negated, that which consists of multiple forms remains. And that has been postulated in various ways by multiple [schools]: for instance, by the Vaibhāṣikas as being directly within the range of perception; by the Vaiśeṣikas, however, as the constituents that originate a composite whole (*avayavin*); and by the Sautrāntikas, as atoms that are eternally beyond perception, yet acting like *piśācas*, intent on imparting their own form upon seeing. In this regard, he says "even atom by atom," etc., in order to refute the atoms postulated by the Vaibhāṣikas.

Just as a single gross [object] does not exist, so too a plurality [of them] does not exist. He states the reason: "because it is not seen even as atoms" (*paramāṇuśo ’py adṛṣṭeḥ*), which means that the form of an atom, being mutually distinct, is not perceived. (114.0) Now, he says—"if there were no parts," etc.—to address the objection that atoms are inferred because a gross object would otherwise be inexplicable: "and if the atom were partless... (*niravayavatve cāṇoḥ*).
Because there would be an absence of the surrounding of multiple atoms,
there could not be any accumulation of forms such as the circle of the earth here. || 114 ||

114.1 This is the intended meaning. First of all, the atom must be regarded as having parts, because—due to its simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms] situated in opposing directions through its parts—there would follow the consequence of its being manifold, just like a gross object, owing to the association with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*). Furthermore, if it were partless—that is, devoid of parts characterized as "directional facets" (*aṃśa*)—then for a single atom, there could be no surrounding or encircling by multiple other atoms; for [if it had no parts], the atom would be... [ed. p.]

In the case of its surrounding [other atoms], for that [atom] which dwells in the midst of the four directions—above and below—the inevitable consequence is that it must possess six parts. For it is not logically possible that the very same intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of this [atom] which is adjacent to the eastern atom is also adjacent to the western atom, because those two would then occupy the same location. Indeed, if the intrinsic nature situated near the eastern atom were to approach the western atom, then that [western atom] too would have to be located there. This same fault applies even if one claims mere facing toward [the other atom] in the absence of actual adjacency.

Furthermore, because it would follow that a mass consists of nothing more than a single atom, there could be no accumulation of forms such as the earth-mandala and so forth here at all. As it has been said: "The form of an atom situated in the middle [of a cluster] is joined [to one atom], located in a distant place [from another], and stands without interval, facing a single atom."

If that very same atom is conceived as being oriented toward another atom, then, this being the case, the accumulation of mountains and so forth would not be possible. [Tattvasaṃgraha 1989–1990 or *Madhyamakālaṃkārakārikā 11–12]

114.2 Therefore, a distinction between the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of those two must necessarily be admitted. And just as there is a distinction between these two, so too there is a distinction between the intrinsic natures of those atoms that are adjacent to the bottom, top, south, and north; thus, by force of logic, the atom is reduced to having six parts. As it is said:
"Because of simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom has six parts. If the six were in the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom. [Viṃśikā 12]
Thus, since the establishment of many does not follow from the non-establishment of one, atoms do not exist. [ed.
114.4 {No Tibetan} "And the Mīmāṃsakas do not necessarily assert atoms" (Ślokavārttika, Anumānapariccheda 183ab).
Thus, the whole (*avayavin*) would not be refuted merely by the refutation of atoms; therefore, the critique of this [whole] is not futile.

[The Madhyamaka Perspective] 3.3.2 Refutation of Vijñaptimātratā "Let it be, then, that the world has the nature of mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*). Yet, as before, that too—whether it be unitary or manifold—is not tenable in form; thus, like a lotus in the sky, it cannot be the object of the conventional usage of 'existent. Since there is no other alternative for a real entity, it must be either one or many. But since it does not cohere in either way, we do not understand how this can be the object of the conventional usage of 'existent.'"

3.3.2.1 Refutation of the Satyākāravāda (or Sākāravāda) [of the Vijñānavādins]: If it be argued that the impossibility of a nature that is both one and many does not apply to consciousness, that is incorrect. For in the case of cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra-jñāna*), the absence of both unitary and manifold forms is as evident as it is in the case of external objects. Indeed, that which the world treats as an external object is precisely what the proponent of aspects regards as cognition. Therefore, whatever sublation applies to its existence as something external applies equally to its existence as something internal. For by means of such sublation, a gross, single entity and a manifold collection of atoms are both refuted.

Furthermore, whether this form—which constitutes the very nature of consciousness—is a single gross entity or is divided into multiple atoms, in either case it is impossible to avoid the refutation that applies to external objects. For that refutation is not based on the object being outside of consciousness, such that it would cease to exist when [the object] exists [within consciousness].

The claim that “the subverting argument based on corporeality applies to the cognizing self (*vijñānātman*), but not to that which is incorporeal” is also insubstantial, because cognition (*vijñāna*) too is corporeal when it possesses the form (*ākāra*) of blue and so forth. For this very spatial extension is what constitutes corporeality. We do not understand why, if this [form] belongs to the external [object], it is designated as "corporeal" but not as "cognition.
3.3.2.2 Refutation of the *Alīkākāravāda* (or *Nirākāravāda*) of the Vijñānavādins.

114.6 It might be thought: "Let this fault apply to those for whom consciousness possesses an aspect (*sākāra-vijñāna*). But for those whose position is that [consciousness] is aspectless (*nirākāra*) and that pleasure and so forth are real (*tāttvika*), how could this [argument of] being neither one nor many be applicable? To this it is replied: Here, consciousness is of the nature of luminosity (*prakāśātmaka*); and no luminosity of theirs is perceived even in a dream apart from the blue and other objects that are themselves manifesting. Furthermore, it is not tenable that blue and other such objects, while they are manifesting, should be unreal (*alīka*) merely because they are like pleasure and so forth.

If it is argued that [pleasure and so forth do not exist] because of the existence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), then by what is this very subverting evidence itself subverted in the case of pleasure and the like? If it is argued that there is an absence of such subversion because pleasure and so forth are formless (*amūrta*), this is not the case; for even that [subverting evidence], as it manifests with spatial extension, cannot be denied. Indeed, when one is exhausted, pleasure is experienced as arising and pervading as many limbs as enter into the water.

Nor is there such a thing as an "extension across space" being experienced in that way, for it would follow that the body itself would possess that same nature; and if there were extension across space, this [consciousness] too would be material, just like the body. Therefore, it should be understood that the Master has not provided a separate refutation, because whether consciousness possesses a form or is formless, it does not escape the criticisms already leveled against external entities.

114.7 Therefore, this remains established: even this consciousness does not deserve to be treated as existent. If that is so, then because both the knower and the known are non-existent, reality would be of a non-existent nature. No; consciousness may exist conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), because conventional reality cannot be denied. If it is argued that since existence has been negated, non-existence follows by necessity, we say no; for non-existence is preceded by existence, and if that [existence] is unestablished, non-existence is likewise unestablished. As it is said: "Non-existence is preceded by existence; existence is preceded by non-existence."

"Therefore, one should not say 'it does not exist,' nor should one conceptualize existence. [Laṅkāvatārasūtra 3.83] Nor is it of a dual nature consisting of both existence and non-existence, because existence and non-existence are contradictory. Nor is it something other than existence and non-existence, having the nature of being neither, for that which is excluded from and outside both is logically impossible. Does it then follow that there is no reality whatsoever? But is this not itself the very reality, namely, the state of being devoid of reality? Thus, this remains established:
Consciousness appears as free from the four extremes;
this is the reality for those who know reality, yet even that reality is not reality in the ultimate sense.
Thus it is said by Jñānapāda: [Ātmasādhanāvatāra 114.8]—
"Let it be, then, that the world has the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and is imperishable," and so forth—[this is] begun [only to be refuted]:

No, because consciousness (*vijñāna*) itself is devoid of a nature that is either one or many. To explain: it is not one, because its perception is variegated due to the distinctions between blue and other colors, because even a single color such as white appears with distinctions of beginning, middle, and end, and because of the differences in the utility of its causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*); for being "many" is defined by nothing more than this. Nor is it many, because parts of the appearance of white and so forth that are like atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not perceived.
And there is no other mode apart from being one or many, because these two are mutually exclusive by their very nature as mutual absences (*anyonyābhāva*).

If it is asked, "If all things are entirely devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*), from where does this observed difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arise?", it has already been explained that this is due solely to preceding and preceding conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) regarding an unexamined unitary essence, since nothing else is perceived.
If it is then argued, "Let there be real existence (*sattva*) for all things in an ultimate sense, because the definition of a real entity (*vastu*) is causal efficiency," [the response follows].

That is not so, because there is no contradiction in accepting existence by way of mere appearance. Selflessness is established precisely through the discernment of characteristics (*lakṣaṇaviveka*) according to the sequence already described, and not by means of a denial even of mere appearance. As it has been said: "Subhūti, form is not one thing and emptiness another; rather, form itself is empty of the characteristic of form," and so forth in detail.

For this very reason, because the entirety of conventional reality appears through the distinction between prior and subsequent [moments], one should not suspect its permanence. As for what was said in the *Daśabhūmikasūtra* (ed. p. 49, 9), "O sons of the Conqueror, that which is called the triple world is representation-only," that was for the purpose of dispelling the determination of external objects on the part of those who are attached to absolute existence; for when that [external object] exists, it is possible to easily effect the refutation of even the determination of mind-only. He says that very thing:

"Relying upon mind-only, one should understand the lack of intrinsic nature in external objects; abiding in the focal point of suchness, one should transcend mind-only. [Laṅkāvatārasūtra 10.256] (with a different *pāda* b).

114.9 Thus far, the existence of subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) has been demonstrated. 115.0 Therefore, because there is an absence of establishing evidence (*sādhakapramāṇa*) and because of the presence of subverting evidence, all things such as the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are devoid of self-nature (*nairātmya*); consequently, this world has a nature constructed solely by conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Concluding [this point], he says: "That which grasps it, etc. (*tad-grāhakādi*, etc.).
Because it is devoid of a grasper and so forth, its nature consists of the conceptualization of independent forms and the like;
it is similar to a city of Gandharvas.
The entire reality, including all that is moving and unmoving. || 115 ||

115.1 By the force of the argument just stated, that [world]—being devoid of a grasper and so forth—is like a city of the Gandharvas; and because it is devoid of any ultimately real cause, it consists of a continuous stream of conceptualization (*kalpanā-santati*), taking the form of independent conceptualizations of forms and other phenomena. Thus, the entity of the moving and the stationary exists. 116.0 Now, one might object: "If such is the reality (*tattva*), then it must be purely pure (*śuddha*). How then can there be *saṃsāra*? And in the absence of that, how could there be purification (*vyavadāna*)? In response to this doubt, he says: "The self," and so forth.
This cycle of existence is a continuum of conceptual construction arising from the superimposition of a self and what belongs to a self;
purity is its opposite.
But it should be understood as consisting of its own essential nature alone. || 116 ||

116.1. In that very mind, which is devoid of the four extremes (*catuḥkoṭi*), saṃsāra consists of the form of a stream of conceptualization (*vikalpasantāna*) through the superimposition (*āropa*) of a self (*ātman*) and so forth; whereas purity, namely liberation (*mokṣa*), should be understood as abiding solely in the nature of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is the opposite of the superimposition of a self and so forth. For this very reason it has been said: "One should strive for purity from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāśuddhau yatitavyam*). For instance, a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that determines external objects is common and conducive to worldly existence (*bhava*) because it is erroneous (*bhrānta*); however, by abiding solely in its own nature and being non-erroneous, it is non-conceptual and thus has the character of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is completely pure. As it has been said:
"Even conceptual construction is accepted as being self-cognizing, but not as having an object, because it is a mental construction. (Pramāṇasamuccaya 1.7ab).
Furthermore, passion and the like, while superimposing [attributes], are established as having the nature of a corrupted mind. As it is said in the *Śrīparamādya*:
Passion, hatred, and delusion—these three have become poison. They attain the state of poison when practiced in an improper manner;
however, when practiced for the sake of immortality, they attain the state of nectar.
Thus, having turned conceptual construction away from the fault of determining external objects, yogins must strive to establish it within its own nature.

Therefore, even conceptual construction is indeed non-conceptual with respect to its own nature; thus, all phenomena are pure by their very essence. As it is said: "And there is nothing whatsoever," and so forth.
And herein there is no distinction whatsoever according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) among those whose intrinsic nature is the state of peace;
they are devoid of the forms of the grasped and so forth.
For he is eternally perfected everywhere. || 117 ||

117.1. "Something" refers to the distinction or differentiation such as "this is nirvāṇa, this is saṃsāra; this is the stained state, this is the stainless state; this is to be abandoned, this is to be adopted," and so forth. Such a distinction is not, indeed, not at all tenable according to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) in reality. He states the proof for this with the words beginning "the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*). For this very reason, the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also said: "Nirvāṇa and existence—these two do not exist.
The thorough knowledge of existence itself is called 'nirvāṇa. [Yuktiṣaṣṭikā 6]
"There is not the slightest distinction of saṃsāra from nirvāṇa;
there is not the slightest distinction of nirvāṇa from saṃsāra. (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 25.19)
The Blessed One has also said:

"Subhūti, that which is the suchness of ordinary beings and that which is the suchness of the Tathāgata are one and the same. This is the full extent of the passage, beginning with these words. [Prajñāpāramitā, untraced]

118. Now, if in reality there is no distinction between those things whose nature is the state of peace (*śamabhava*), then how can it be stated that "there is an absence of the forms of the grasped object and so forth everywhere" (117cd)? For the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to a plurality of objects, and it might be objected that it cannot be applied where there is an absence of distinction; anticipating this, he says: "And yet, all is not even anything... and so on. [It is said: "And yet, all is not even anything, because of the conceptualization of its own nature as a manifestation."
Nor can there be anything other than the mind that is the "I"; therefore, there is no such thing as a self (ātman) and so forth. || 118 ||

[Ed. p. 113] 118.1 However, conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), there is indeed a distinction between those things whose intrinsic nature is peace and existence (as noted in 117b). Therefore, that which is the nature of the appearance of conventional objects is nothing other than conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*). The word "all" (*sarva*) has as its object a distinction superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Thus, the meaning is that in everything of such a nature, the negation of an ultimate distinction (*tāttvika-bheda*) is being established. In this way, even the moving and the non-moving are not other than the conceptual construction of the nature of their own appearance.

3.5 Refutation of the View of a Self (ātmadarśana) 118.2 Objection: If the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*) were to possess a true object, then because there would be no absence of self (*nairātmya*), existence (*bhava*) would necessarily exist; how then could there be no distinction between those whose nature is existence and those whose nature is peace (*śama*)? Response: That is not so. For the view of a self is of two kinds: that which is produced by volitional conditioning (*ābhisamskārika*) and that which is innate (*sahaja*).

In this regard, for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, there is the "conditioned" (*ābhisaṃskārika*) view of self, which arises from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the study of the treatises of Kaṇāda and others that designate a self as distinct from the body and so forth—an eternal and omnipresent agent of auspicious and inauspicious karma and enjoyer of its fruits. On the other hand, there is the "innate" (*sahaja*) view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), common to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), which consists of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) that determines the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantati*)—under the influence of beginningless ignorance and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—as having a stable grasper and so forth.
3.5.1 Refutation of the Conceptually Constructed (*ābhisaṃskārika*) View of Self 3.5.1.1 Absence of Valid Means of Proof (*sādhakapramāṇa*) for It

In that regard, concerning the first position, there is first of all no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the self (*ātman*). For the self is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the cognitions of the eyes and other senses are restricted to the fivefold objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Nor is it perceived through inference (*anumāna*), because of the absence of any logical mark (*liṅga*) consisting of either an effect (*kārya*) or an essential nature (*svabhāva*). This is because, since the self is eternally beyond the senses (*nityaparokṣa*) and devoid of spatial or temporal variation, the relationship of producer and produced—characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—cannot be established with respect to anything; thus, there is an absence of a mark consisting of an effect. [Regarding] the subject (*dharmin*)... [text fragment]

Furthermore, because [the self] is unestablished (*asiddha*), it cannot function as an essential nature (*svabhāva*) as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Nor is any other positive probative mark possible by which an inference of this [self] might occur. Moreover, for any other mark you propose, it must be pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*). Since the self, which is the probandum, is not established anywhere, its status as a pervader (*vyāpaka*) is not certain; therefore, it is impossible to ascertain that anything is pervaded by it. Thus, no logical mark whatsoever is tenable for this [self].

118.3 One might object: "Granted that visual and other sensory cognitions, or inference, may not be the means of establishing [the self], yet there certainly exists a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) in the form of the 'I-notion' (*ahaṃpratyaya*) which ascertains the self. Anticipating this, he says: "And there is nothing other than the mind," and so forth. There could not possibly exist any self or the like, distinct from the mind, that would be the object of the 'I-notion'—that is, the referent of the thought "I"—because the 'I-notion' has the body and such as its object.

The notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) arises in such forms as "I am black," "I am stout," or "I am going. Now, blackness or stoutness cannot be a property of this [self] if it is distinct from the body; nor is the action of going—which conforms to a material substance—possible for that which is all-pervading and formless. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to consider this [notion] figurative, like the cognition of a lion in a boy, because there is no failure [of the primary sense]. And when there is no failure, it is not right to assume a figurative application, lest it lead to the collapse of primary linguistic usage.
118.5 Therefore, this remains established: since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the self, its fitness for the practical usage of existence has indeed vanished.

[3.5.1.2] However, due to the presence of subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhakapramāṇa*), its non-existence alone is logical. For if the self were to exist, it would have to be either of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpa*) or of the nature of non-consciousness (*abodharūpa*). In the first case, the consequence of the futility of the eyes and other sense organs is unavoidable. Indeed, there can be no utility for the eyes and so forth in a permanent self whose nature is the perception of form and other objects.
Non-perception subverts the existence of the self, even though its nature is that of non-cognition.

For it is a rule that when something which has reached the conditions for perception is not perceived in a certain place, its absence there must be asserted, as in the case of a horn on a horse's head. Now, the self—which has reached the conditions for perception—is not perceived within the body and so forth.

118.7 But surely it is precisely undesirable for those who maintain that the self exists to claim that the body and so forth are its locus. As it has been said: "To whom does the self belong in the body? [Nyāyavārttika ad 3.1.1; p. 320, 8–9 (or p. 325, 23)]. And if such a [self] is refuted, there is nothing undesirable [in our position].

True. We do not deny the locus (*adheya*) here, but rather the correlate (*saṃsargin*). For it is the correlate alone that is denied everywhere through non-perception (*anupalambha*), since even a pot or the like, which is to be denied, is a correlate. Furthermore, the locus itself does not become the correlate; otherwise, because there would be no correlation with the self (*ātman*) as a non-locus, even the possession of a self (*sātmakatva*) by the body and so forth would not exist.
Nor is the body and so forth presented here as the locus for the object of negation, but rather [as the locus] for non-perception and the conventional usage of negation; thus there is no fault.

Now, this non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is certainly not the mere absence of apprehension, because that cannot function as a means of proof (*sādhana*). Nor does it have the nature of the apprehension of another object associated with the same cognition; for while something may be associated with the self in a single cognition, there is no other distinct object experienced that has become the domain of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). Thus, the apprehension of that [self] itself is its non-apprehension [of anything else].

Now, if the referent of the "I" (*asmadartha*) were not perceived as distinct from the body and so forth, the cognition "my body" would not occur. Yet this cognition does exist. Therefore, the referent of the "I" must be regarded as being perceived precisely as distinct from the body and so forth. Why, then, is it said that it is not apprehended? This is incorrect. For a cognition arises even while conceiving a distinction that does not exist, such as "the body of a stone statue. Moreover, mere cognition is not what constitutes apprehension here; rather, it is the cognition regarded as perceptual.

Moreover, this [cognition] is not itself a perception, because it is no different from the non-perceptual cognition that [the body] is distinct from the body of a stone statue (*śilāputraka*); for if this [cognition], which is indistinguishable from that, were perceptual, it would follow that the latter too would be perceptual, and if it were perceptual, it would entail that it serves as a basis for establishing a separate entity. And just as there is the cognition "my body" and so forth, so too does the cognition "my self" certainly occur.

Therefore, this "beloved of the gods" (the opponent), while validating another cognition that establishes a distinction from our own object, ought by parity of reasoning to validate this [cognition of the stone statue] as well, and in so doing, he would have to establish another self. Or, if he subsumes this cognition under the category of cognitions establishing a distinction from the body of a stone statue, he should likewise subsume his own self under that same category, thinking, "my body and so forth. Enough of this prolixity.
Consequently, it remains established: non-apprehension does not tolerate a self that is non-conscious in nature.
118.8 Therefore, it is established that its non-existence alone is logical.
% 3.5.2 Refutation of the Innate (sahaja) View of the Self

118.9 Now, raising the objection: "How can the innate view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is established for all the world, be denied? he says: "And not from the mind," and so forth. This is the intended meaning: since, according to the sequence already described, there is an absence of all entities such as the knower and the known, there could not possibly exist anything other than the mind—as previously described—that could serve as the object of the ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form of a stable grasper or the like, such that one might think "I am. Therefore, for this reason, the mind itself, as previously stated, is the object of the ego-conception.

Therefore, because the self (*ātman*) is non-existent in every respect, the vision of a self is unreal in its object, just like the cognition of [non-existent] hair and so forth. Consequently, it is not the case that because existence (*bhava*) exists when there is no selflessness (*nairātmya*), there is an absence of the negation of difference between those things whose nature consists of both existence and its cessation (*bhavaśama*).
Concluding this, while establishing precisely the non-difference as previously stated, he says: "That which is form," and so forth.
Whatever form is perceived, that very thing is its own innate nature;
that is the non-differentiation of the cognition regarding it.
The non-differentiation of all phenomena. || 119 ||

119.1 And that form or object which is apprehended by that mind is not established as external to the mind due to the reasoning just stated. Therefore, what could its own nature be, since there is nothing other than the form perceived by the mind? It is precisely that form which was apprehended by the mind.

And from that follows the investigation: since difference is not established, that mind which conceives of non-difference—that mental act of conceiving non-difference—is the cause by which all entities, apprehended by a mind [perceiving] non-differently, possess nothing other than their own innate non-distinct form. Thus, their very non-difference is established through reasoning.

Alternatively: that which is conventionally apprehended by the foolish has its own true, essential nature as it is apprehended by the wise who are free from error; and that very thing is its own essential nature. Since this is so, therefore, because of the realization through cognition that there is no differentiation among all things—whose nature consists of peace and existence—due to their non-difference in having emptiness as their single form, all phenomena are non-distinct.
As it has been said:
A single entity is the intrinsic nature of all entities; all entities have the intrinsic nature of a single entity.
He by whom one entity is seen in its true reality [sees all].
"By him all things have been seen according to reality. [Locus classicus untraced; see Sferra 2003: 69].
It has also been stated by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"Reality is not perceived apart from the conventional."
"Conventional reality is said to be emptiness, for emptiness itself is indeed conventional reality" (*Bodhicittavivaraṇa* 67cd–68ab).
Elucidating the point that "everything is not anything at all," he says: "It appears," and so forth.
Whatever object appears, and whatever else is the locus of conceptual construction—
due to the absence of separation from each of those.
And for this reason, nothing whatsoever exists as mutually dependent.

120.1 That which appears—that is, the object consisting of form and so forth which manifests as something to be grasped (*grāhya*), and whatever other thing consists of the nature of a grasper (*grāhaka*) as the object of the ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*), being the locus and support of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—because of the absence of that very separation, that state of being distinct, and that plurality (*nānātva*) between each such object and grasper, nothing is differentiated from anything else. And for this reason, "nothing" means that everything is not anything at all, because in ultimate reality it has the nature of mere emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The point is that plurality is merely conceptual.
120.2 For this very reason, the Master Dignāga said:
"The knowledge of ordinary beings that is naturally pure is described by the word 'Buddha,' just as a Bodhisattva is a Victor. [Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārthasaṃgraha 37]

Thus, for this very reason, it is stated even in the *Paramādya*: "All sentient beings possess the tathāgatagarbha by virtue of having the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra as their universal self. [Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā, ed. p. 97, 13–14]

120.3 Therefore, because of the equality of being enlightened and unenlightened in reality (*tattvataḥ*), there is no difference between Buddhas and sentient beings, since the difference exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*). And thus, one should understand that what was stated—that the entire world has been made fully awakened (verse 109cd)—is logical, because the world is pure by nature (*svabhāvaśuddhatvāt*). However, through the practice of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must be purified, because of the fault of superimposing distinctions such as "Buddha" and so forth based on mental fabrication (*kalpanāvaśāt*).

In the same way, it should be understood that within one's own mantra—which has brought about the realization of the entire interior of the world—and within its *bindu*, the visualization of the maṇḍala-cakra, which is the very nature of the universe, is entirely logical; for in the absence of objects of knowledge and so forth, it arises precisely as one's own self-manifestation (*svapratibhāsa*). Thus, everything is well-established.
